policy.impact: Critical: established audit/data loss or compromise; High: incorrect installation/publication or potential serious exposure; Medium: visible, administratively repairable state/operation errors; Low: diagnostic/documentation effects or discounted candidates.
policy.uncertainty: An unconfirmed trigger/consumer lowers the supported potential impact by one level; an excluded replay alone does not negate an applicable historical witness.
policy.closed_records: Refuted, withdrawn and accepted-behavior references receive Low administrative priority and remain non-actionable. They are not promoted into active defects.
policy.aliases: Use the canonical finding's scoped severity; aliases add no defect credit.
policy.proposals: Rate the consequence the proposal addresses, independently of whether the design comparison was withdrawn.
policy.security: Defensive source and existing-evidence review only; no new security or interrupted-archive reproductions.

C:D17.basis: Authenticated metadata succeeds but protected artifact bytes cannot be downloaded; this blocks installation and is recoverable by fixing the request authentication.

C:D18.basis: Existing evidence shows invalid artifact bytes reported as successfully extracted and activated. This is a false installation result; decoder and broader archive-safety claims remain outside scope.

C:D20.basis: Repository credentials can reach a different origin or redirect hop. This rates potential credential disclosure, not an observed production compromise; the origin policy remains open.

C:D22.basis: Only digest spelling differs: uppercase hexadecimal rejects valid bytes. No integrity bypass is alleged, and real-registry prevalence remains unconfirmed.

C:D23.basis: An invalid attribute is silently ignored. The demonstrated consequence is missing validation/diagnostics; no authentication bypass is established.

C:D26.basis: A formerly declared web application remains after replacement and later uninstall, requiring administrator cleanup. Upgrade ownership policy remains unresolved.

C:D30.basis: The service/listing selects a different deep-build tag while the checked installer selects the expected artifact. The demonstrated impact is misleading listing order.

G:D10.basis: Abnormal termination leaves a durable history row with start values rather than the known action progress/outcome. This impairs administrative diagnosis; fresh process-death qualification remains open.

G:D14.basis: A dependency can retain changes when its parent rolls back. This is an installation-state/atomicity policy consequence, not a defect under the current NoJournal working assumption.

G:D15.basis: A documented archive format does not load, while the equivalent supported extension works. The failure is visible and an administrator can rename/use a supported input.

G:D16.basis: The wrong-module archive gives an internal error, a false commit marker in NoTransaction mode and leftover extracted files. No unwanted module-manifest installation is inferred.

G:D17.basis: Relative-path acceptance is evidenced, but loading an unintended module or violating a required refusal is not established. This rates the limited interface/documentation candidate.

G:D26.basis: An unfinished record can report uncommitted after changes were retained, misleading audit/recovery decisions. The abnormal-end outcome policy and exact fresh witness remain open.

G:D27.basis: Finalizing an unfinished record prevents ordinary correction and misstates its lifecycle state. This is a recoverable history-management consequence, conditional on the open finalization policy.

G:I2.basis: A stopped load can leave a temporary registry entry. The broader claim of always winning later resolution was narrowed; unqualified downstream selection keeps this below Medium.

G:I4.basis: Programmatic global-history rows cannot identify their namespace/record ID, limiting reliable attribution. Whether that API shape must change remains an owner question.

G:I5.basis: A processor compile error could be reported as successful compilation. High-impact silent incomplete work is discounted one level because a supported failing compile entry remains unconfirmed.

G:I6.basis: External files/effects can remain after database rollback and require reconciliation. This is a conditional compensation-policy consequence; database transactions alone never promised filesystem rollback.

G:I8.basis: The NoLock argument may enable compile locking rather than bypass it. The anticipated effect is contention/timeouts, discounted from Medium because the actual competing compile schedule is unqualified.

G:OBS-L16.basis: A failed legacy install may misreport retained changes as uncommitted. The Medium audit consequence is discounted because the exact legacy-provider path remains unqualified.

G:OBS-H7.basis: Dependency source is hidden in an install-only display while the stored source remains available. This is a display/policy record, not a demonstrated installation error.

G:OBS-H12.basis: A failed maintenance purge could stop the requested command. The recoverable Medium command failure is discounted because an ordinary failing provider trigger is unconfirmed.

G:OBS-H13.basis: Shared temporary history clearing could lose or mix another namespace's in-progress audit records. Potential Critical data loss is discounted one level because the concurrent trigger is unconfirmed.

G:OBS-H15.basis: A skipped self-uninstall may still report success and exit the shell. This rates the limited diagnostic/control-flow candidate; the full interactive outcome remains unqualified.

G:D7.basis: The raw-status display is documented and this allegation is withdrawn. Low labels the retained documentation/review record; no current defect is asserted.

G:OBS-H9.basis: Unconfirmed global deletion is documented behavior and the allegation is withdrawn. Low labels the policy reference, not a newly alleged unsafe-delete defect.

G:OBS-H10.basis: The claimed empty namespace groups were refuted. Low is administrative priority for the closed display record; no surviving product consequence is asserted.

G:OBS-L15.basis: Temporary LoadedResource lifetime is outside the reviewed functional contract. No material consequence through a supported caller is established; this remains a scoped reference record.

G:OOS-1.basis: Unquoted URL/branch values at a shell boundary present potential command injection. Potential Critical compromise is discounted because reachability/exploitation is unconfirmed; defensive review only.

G:OOS-2.basis: A verify phase has a history-coverage difference, but phase commands are excluded by the recorded history contract. This rates the observability/scope reference without reopening a defect.

G:OOS-3.basis: A skipped method is displayed as passed. Only misleading test-count output is established, not an incorrect command verdict or a demonstrated faulty release.

P:F-DEP-4.basis: A dependency-scope comment contradicts the implemented/tested behavior. This is documentation drift.

P:F-DEP-5.basis: A test comment still describes an already-fixed intersection edge case. This is stale documentation.

P:F-DEP-6.basis: Empty/swallowing assertions weaken test evidence. No additional product failure follows from the test gap alone.

P:F-HIST-2.basis: A developer-mode crash retains the module but leaves misleading commit/name history fields, impairing recovery diagnosis. The exact fresh crash-in-dependency gate remains open.

P:F-HIST-4.basis: The retained record concerns an operator-selected terminal commit and its documentation. It does not establish a product defect under an accepted supported-input contract.

P:F-HIST-7.basis: A narrow commit-to-marker window can misreport retained work. Medium audit impact is discounted because the deterministic witness uses a patched stall and the graceful-stop cause remains unidentified.

P:F-HIST-8.basis: Restart can leave a misleading, editable unfinished audit row after changes survived. This affects administrative recovery; no fresh restart witness is claimed.

P:F-INST-11.basis: Help/README descriptions disagree about developer bypass and reinstall version. This is documentation and unresolved-intent clarification, not a new runtime defect.

P:F-INST-2.basis: The mirror-role-change comment promises unsupported behavior and a test can skip silently. The retained issue is documentation/test quality.

P:F-INST-3.basis: Update interruption/failure tests assert too little. This rates a coverage gap without inventing another product failure.

P:F-LOAD-1.basis: A failed clone is reported later as a missing manifest, obscuring its cause. The demonstrated issue is misleading diagnostics; the URL/shell boundary is not reprobed.

P:F-LOAD-2.basis: URL loads retain a clone in a temporary directory used by later reload/sync, creating persistent cleanup/source-location dependence. No URL/shell reproduction was run in this review.

P:F-LOAD-3.basis: A failed archive load can replace installed source files while database state rolls back, requiring administrator reconciliation. The excluded archive entry is not exercised or widened to irreversible business-data loss.

P:F-NSP-1.basis: Enable can report success despite installer failure, leaving the namespace incompletely enabled. This is visible, administratively repairable installation misbehavior.

P:F-NSP-10.basis: Legacy module records may remain unmigrated. Medium upgrade-management impact is discounted because the evidence uses simulated legacy records rather than a fully qualified old installation.

P:F-NSP-11.basis: Enable-community returns success after a component failure. Medium partial-enable impact is discounted because the exact current failure/consumer gate remains unqualified.

P:F-NSP-3.basis: Version help omits the build labels that the command prints. This is display/documentation drift.

P:F-NSP-5.basis: Installing through an existing code mapping can update shared source code and leave ownership/unmap state inconsistent. Existing observations support an administrator-repairable mapping defect.

P:F-NSP-7.basis: An ambiguous shared-code source can produce the wrong owner and skip repository mapping/warnings. This affects namespace administration; source-selection policy remains open.

P:F-NSP-8.basis: The argument-slot error causes extra configuration activations without a demonstrated final-state difference. A collation/data consequence is not asserted.

P:F-NSP-9.basis: Upgrade CLI scripts may be written under an unexpanded placeholder instead of installed. Medium missing-command impact is discounted because a genuine legacy-upgrade producer remains unqualified.

P:F-REPO-1.basis: The selected token-auth protocol is ignored, causing valid authenticated registry requests to fail. No credential disclosure to a new destination is alleged for this entry.

P:F-REPO-10.basis: Publication can go to the wrong configured registry despite its publish flag. This is an incorrect publication destination with potential source exposure; no production disclosure is claimed.

P:F-REPO-11.basis: Changing an ORAS address retains credentials that can reach the new host. Potential Critical credential exposure is discounted for the unqualified delivery/authorization policy; source/existing-evidence review only.

P:F-REPO-12.basis: A deployed platform-tagged version cannot be unpublished using its version. This breaks a registry-management operation and needs an administrator workaround.

P:F-REPO-2.basis: Documented SSL and publication endpoint options are ignored, preventing the intended registry configuration. No TLS-verification bypass or actual disclosure is inferred.

P:F-REPO-3.basis: Publish selection help is stale relative to the supported fallback policy. This is documentation drift.

P:F-REPO-6.basis: The claimed unrelated-class dispatch is unreachable through the supported parser and was refuted. Low labels the closed review record, not a surviving code-execution vulnerability.

P:F-REPO-7.basis: A disabled registry can still be contacted with credentials or selected for publication. Potential Critical exposure is discounted because harmful-recipient/authorization consequences are unconfirmed.

P:F-REPO-9.basis: An invalid repository type prompts rather than producing the intended diagnostic and can consume subsequent script input. No unrelated-class dispatch is inferred.

P:F-RES-2.basis: The documented register phase is absent or silently ineffective in a sequence. The established scope is an incomplete documented option and misleading status.

P:F-RES-3.basis: A developer-mode deployment command changes class/source availability despite saying it will only report. The shown effects require source reload/administrator repair; irreversible business-data loss is not established.

P:F-RES-4.basis: A successful package command omits its output-file location without verbosity. This is missing user-facing information.

P:F-RES-5.basis: Command-file help specifies the wrong extension/JSON shape. This is documentation that misleads users into invalid inputs.

P:F-RES-6.basis: An exec example promises a persistent namespace change that is deliberately isolated. This is a documentation error.

P:F-RES-7.basis: Long names are truncated in produced packages, making required artifacts unusable or missing under the expected name. The original input remains available; irreversible source-data loss is not asserted.

P:F-RES-8.basis: Nested quiet output can close the outer null device and fail. Medium command failure is discounted because this audit has not qualified the ordinary nested command/reader beyond inherited test evidence.

P:F-SYNC-2.basis: The first sync after skip-sync deliberately absorbs a baseline; the flag documentation should disclose this. This is a documentation record.

P:F-UNIN-10.basis: Cleanup leaves cache indices that prevent later filesystem-registry creation until they are repaired. This is recoverable administrative breakage.

P:F-UNIN-11.basis: Level-zero self-Clean prints an orphan warning and may skip its expected hooks. The confirmed warning is misleading; the broader hook consequence remains unqualified.

P:F-UNIN-3.basis: Aliases skip self-uninstall safeguards and can leave the package manager unusable until reinstalled. Existing evidence supports administrative recovery impact, not a new authorization/exploitation claim.

P:F-UNIN-7.basis: Untyped orphan listings contain system/mapped items that should not be treated as user-owned cleanup targets. Only misleading inventory output is established.

P:F-UNIN-8.basis: Recursive uninstall can remove the package manager mid-operation and leave partial cleanup/records behind. Core package-management operations remain unavailable until recovery.

G:D1.basis: A parent rollback removes a dependency's durable audit record entirely. The through-product witness establishes audit-data loss, which the G5 severity convention rates Critical.

G:D2.basis: A documented version-part filter can turn a filtered delete into deletion of the entire history. The witness establishes unintended loss of unrelated persisted audit data.

G:D25.basis: A caller rollback removes the action's durable history. Critical is the conditional audit-data-loss impact if caller-survival is required; Q-05 remains unresolved.

C:D32.basis: An explicit requested-version install succeeds with another version's callable bytes. This is a wrong installation result, not merely stale listing text.

P:F-REPO-4.basis: Config delete restores a prior assigned value instead of the documented default, changing effective configuration. This is administrator-repairable behavior, not merely cosmetic text.

P:F-LOAD-4.basis: An ordinary load returns failure after its changes commit, leaving installed code and a failed command result. This can misdirect scripts and recovery even though the trigger is an after-install message.
